opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't really about programming at first. I got obsessed with the idea of AI itself. I was around fourteen, and I had this realization that if you could build something that thinks, something that could actually do research and solve problems, that would be the most leveraged thing a person could possibly work on. Every other problem you might care about, curing diseases, science, anything, becomes easier if you crack that one.

So programming was just the means to an end. I didn't come from a family of engineers or anything like that. I just figured, okay, if I want to work on this, I need to be able to build things, so I'd better learn to code. I started teaching myself, reading papers I barely understood at first, implementing things, breaking things, and slowly it clicked.

And I think that framing really helped me. Because I wasn't learning programming for its own sake, I was always pulling toward a goal. Every new thing I learned was in service of "can I get closer to building something that actually reasons?" That kept me going through all the boring and frustrating parts. When you're fourteen and you've decided this is the most important problem in the world, you're willing to stay up very late debugging.

r001.rationale: He says he was driven by the idea of AI and learned to code because he wanted to build something that could think and solve problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't programming that motivated me, it was AI. Programming was just the thing in the way. When I was about 14 I'd gotten really into the idea that you could build something that actually thinks, and at the time, around 2013 or 2014, deep learning was starting to show up in things like image recognition and speech. I remember reading about it and thinking, this is the most important thing a person could work on. If you could build a system that could reason and learn, every other problem becomes downstream of that.

So I went looking for how to do it, and the answer was obviously: you have to be able to write code. I didn't have any formal background. I taught myself Python from online courses and whatever tutorials I could find, and pretty quickly I was trying to implement neural networks from scratch, badly, and then reading the research papers to understand why mine didn't work. I was emailing researchers I'd read about, asking questions that were probably naive, and a surprising number of them wrote back.

I think the thing that kept me going was that I was impatient. I didn't want to wait until I was 22 with a degree to start working on this. It felt like the field was moving, and I wanted to be part of it now rather than later. Programming was the entry fee, so I paid it. And then once you're in it, you start to actually enjoy the craft itself, but that came second.

r001.rationale: He says it was AI—not programming—that motivated him, explaining that he learned to code because it was necessary to build systems that think, reason, and learn.

astra-6.text: For me, programming was a means to an end. I was fascinated by AI and wanted to understand how to build it. Learning to code was the first step toward being able to experiment with those ideas myself, rather than just reading about them.

r001.rationale: The response says he was fascinated by AI and learned to code so he could understand how to build it himself, identifying AI as his motivation.

sol-6.1.text: I was fascinated by the idea that intelligence could be understood and recreated. If you could build something that learns and solves problems, that seemed like an incredibly powerful thing to work on. Programming was the practical starting point—it let me go from being curious about AI to actually experimenting with it myself.

r001.rationale: The response says he was fascinated by recreating intelligence and saw programming as a way to experiment with AI, communicating that pursuing AI motivated him to learn programming.
